title: Eyes turned around
hookLine: a child stares at a light bulb, squeezes her eyes shut, and finds a glowing shape still floating there
carry: turn the eyes around, toward the self within

lines: STARE AT THE LIGHT. SHUT THE EYES.
NOT A SIDE EFFECT. THE SECOND HALF.
cards: A child lies on her bed staring up at the light bulb, because someone told her not to. Then she squeezes her eyes shut.
And there it is: a glowing shape floating in the dark behind her eyelids, green, then purple, drifting when she moves her eyes. She opens them, stares again, shuts them again, delighted. It's a game.
In trataka, the same thing happens, and it isn't treated as a side effect. Some teachers make it the second half.

teach.h: OUTER TRATAKA: EYES OPEN, ON THE FLAME.
teach.b: Some teachers of trataka describe it in two parts. Outer trataka is the gaze on the flame or the mark, eyes open.

teach.h: INNER TRATAKA: THE IMAGE BEHIND THE LIDS.
teach.b: Inner trataka begins when the eyes close: the image left behind is held in attention, gently, for as long as it lasts.

When it fades, some teachers say to keep looking into the place where it was, or to open the eyes and gaze again. The practice moves the same object from in front of the eyes to behind them. Why bother?
In the Katha Upanishad, Death, still teaching the boy Nachiketas, names the problem the second half answers.
In paraphrase: the Self-existent one pierced the openings of the senses outward, so a person looks outward, and not at the Self within.
But a certain wise one, wanting the deathless, turned the eyes around and saw the Self within. Eyes turned around: that's the heart of it.

teach.h: THE SENSES WERE MADE TO FACE OUT.
teach.b: The senses are made to face out, sight especially, running ahead of us all day to the next screen, the next face, the next sign. The verse doesn't blame the eyes for that. It says that's how they were made.

teach.h: THE WISE ONE TURNED THE EYES AROUND, TOWARD THE SELF.
teach.b: Then it describes someone who, for once, turns them back, toward the atman, the Self, the same witness that stays awake in sleep.

teach.h: FROM THE FLAME OUT THERE TO THE FLAME IN HERE.
teach.b: Trataka does this in a very literal, very small way. The outer gaze gathers attention onto one point. Then the eyelids close, and that same gathered attention points inward at an image that exists only on the inside.
It isn't the Upanishad's whole vision, only a training run: a minute of turning the eyes around.

how: Some teachers of trataka pair the open-eyed gaze at a flame with a closed-eyed phase, in which the practitioner holds the after-image in attention until it fades, then gazes again.

o: picturing a flame you have never actually seen
a still gaze at a point, then its image held within
staring at a bright light until you see colors

games.q: outer and inner — tap the pairs.
p: eyes open, gaze on the flame
the image held behind the lids
pierced outward, made to face out

s: in trataka, the glowing shape behind the lids is just a side effect to ignore
some teachers make it the second half: inner trataka holds that image in attention.
the Katha Upanishad says the senses were made to face outward
it says the Self-existent one pierced the openings outward, so a person looks out, not within.
in the Katha Upanishad, people look outward simply by their own choice
it says the Self-existent made the openings face outward; the wise one who turns the eyes around is the rare exception.

games.q: you've gazed at the flame, and now your eyes are closed. a glowing shape floats there. what do you do?
o: rub the eyes to clear it away.
hold it in attention until it fades.
games.why: in inner trataka the after-image is the object: held gently until it fades, then the gaze begins again.

practice: Set a candle flame or a small, bright mark at eye level, never the sun, and gaze at it softly for a few breaths, blinking when you need to.
Then close the eyes and hold the image it left behind without squinting or chasing it, noticing its color, where it drifts, how it fades.
When it's gone, rest in the dark where it was for a breath or two, then open the eyes and gaze again.

wordCard.voice: Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, both halves: the flame in front of the eyes, and the image held behind them.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: avritta-chakshuh, with eyes turned around. The Katha Upanishad's phrase for the wise one who looked within.

carryVoice: Your line: turn the eyes around, toward the Self within. The flame out there, the flame in here. Until tomorrow.
